papers.title: Prospects of Detecting Cosmological Domain Walls in the Cosmic Microwave Background
papers.authors: Berkin Gürbüz, Robert Brandenberger, Yitian Sun
papers.abstract: Topological defects are a generic prediction of field theories with spontaneously broken symmetries, and domain walls, the two-dimensional defects left by a broken discrete symmetry, are among the simplest. We study the imprint of dark, purely gravitationally interacting domain walls on the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB), in the regime where a low symmetry-breaking scale $\eta$ allows the walls to evade the Zel'dovich overclosure bound while remaining cosmologically relevant. The relativistic repulsion of matter by a planar wall carves out an evacuated void bounded by an overdense shell, and we compute the resulting photon deflection field analytically for walls both aligned with and arbitrarily inclined to the line of sight. The deflection stamps coherent, strongly non-Gaussian distortions onto the temperature sky, with a characteristic two-peak structure set by the relativistic displacement scale and an inclination dependence that vanishes for face-on walls. Because these signatures are localised and anisotropic, they are poorly captured by two-point statistics; we therefore analyse them with a curvelet/wavelet decomposition matched to the wall's geometry, and with simulation-based inference, training a Neural Posterior Estimator (NPE) to recover the scattering redshift $z$, energy scale $\eta$, and inclination $\theta$, and a Neural Ratio Estimator (NRE) to evaluate the likelihood-ratio test statistic for limit-setting. Casting these methods as sensitivity forecasts for a South Pole Telescope-like (SPT) survey, we find that the curvelet and wavelet statistical thresholds populate a common $\eta \sim 10-100$ MeV band over the accessible redshift range. The neural-ratio sensitivity curve, which exploits the full map morphology, reaches a factor 1.3-1.9 lower in $\eta$ at $z \gtrsim 20$, or $\sim 2-7$ in the wall tension, landing essentially on the per-resolution-element noise floor.

ai.summary: The paper asks whether dark, gravitationally interacting planar domain walls (low symmetry-breaking scale $\eta$, evading the Zel'dovich bound) can be detected through CMB lensing. The authors compute the relativistic matter displacement around a wall (an evacuated void bounded by an overdense shell, with no shell crossing), then analytically/numerically derive the photon deflection for walls of finite extent at arbitrary inclination, using the Born approximation. They apply the deflection to Gaussian CMB maps and analyse them with curvelet/wavelet statistics and simulation-based inference (NPE for $z,\eta,\theta$; NRE for a likelihood-ratio test). They forecast idealized sensitivity for an SPT-3G-like survey, with no foregrounds or LCDM lensing.
conclusions: Wall repulsion gives a void plus overdense shell; the deflection is line-like, non-Gaussian, with a two-peak structure set by the displacement scale $\psi(z)$, and vanishes for face-on walls by mass conservation.
Curvelet and wavelet statistics reach a common $\eta\sim10$-$100$ MeV detectability band over the accessible redshift range.
The neural ratio estimator is a factor 1.3-1.9 deeper in $\eta$ at $z\gtrsim20$ (~2-7 in tension), close to the noise floor.
NPE shows a $z$-$\eta$ degeneracy in a single patch while recovering $\theta$ independently; the forecasts are idealized (single aligned wall, Gaussian sky, no foregrounds).

papers.title: AMICO galaxy clusters in KiDS-1000: Cosmological constraints from the two-point correlation function
papers.authors: Massimiliano Romanello, Giorgio Francesco Lesci, Federico Marulli, Lauro Moscardini, Carlo Giocoli, Matteo Maturi, Mario Radovich, Sandro Bardelli, Gianluca Castignani, Hendrik Hildebrandt, Lorenzo Ingoglia, Shahab Joudaki, Emanuella Puddu, Mauro Sereno
papers.abstract: In this paper we study the clustering properties of an optically identified photometric galaxy cluster catalogue from KiDS-1000. The sample was identified by the AMICO algorithm and consists of 9049 clusters with $S/N\geq3.5$, in the redshift range $0.1\leq z<0.8$, spread over an effective area of 838.78 deg$^2$. Clusters are selected according to their observed intrinsic richness, with thresholds of $\lambda^*{obs}\geq 20,25,30$ within $0.10\leq z<0.30$, $0.30\leq z<0.45$ and $0.45\leq z<0.80$, respectively. We measure the multipoles of the two-point correlation function over different ranges of scales from 5 $h^{-1}$ Mpc to 150 $h^{-1}$ Mpc. We model the clustering signal in the context of the $\Lambda$CDM cosmology, accounting for the main observational effects, such RSDs and photo-$z$ uncertainties. The effective bias of the cluster sample is estimated via a mass-richness scaling relation. For the MCMC analysis, we adopt Gaussian priors on the parameters of the mass-richness scaling relation, and broad, uniform priors to derive cosmological constraints on the cold matter density parameter, the power spectrum amplitude and the structure growth parameter, $S_8\equiv\sigma_8 \sqrt{\Omega{m}/0.3}$. Specifically, we find $\Omega_{m}=0.24^{+0.02}{-0.02}$ and $\sigma_8=0.86^{+0.13}{-0.10}$ representing an improvement in precision over both the 2D and 3D AMICO clustering analyses performed on the previous KiDS data release. Moreover, we obtain $S_8=0.77^{+0.10}_{-0.08}$ in $1\sigma$ agreement with the AMICO KiDS-1000 number counts constraints estimated from the same catalogue, as well as with some results from external early- and late-Universe data sets. Our work strengthens the potential of cluster clustering as a complementary and competitive probe, to be included and further developed with the final KiDS-Legacy data release, and in other future Stage-IV photometric redshift surveys.

ai.summary: The paper measures the two-point correlation function multipoles (monopole, quadrupole, hexadecapole) of 9049 AMICO-selected optical galaxy clusters in KiDS-1000 (0.1≤z<0.8, 838.78 deg²) in three redshift bins, over 5–150 h^-1 Mpc. The model uses a linear-theory (Eisenstein-Hu) Kaiser plus dispersion-model power spectrum. It includes geometric distortions, photo-z damping (σ_z=0.014(1+z)) and the AMICO redshift discretisation. The effective bias comes from a mass-richness scaling relation (Tinker bias) with Gaussian priors from the earlier weak-lensing and number-count calibration. Covariances come from 500 bootstraps. An MCMC in ΛCDM gives constraints on Ω_m, σ_8 and S_8 that are more precise than the earlier KiDS-DR3 clustering analyses, and consistent with the KiDS-1000 cluster abundance results.
conclusions: Ω_m=0.24±0.02 and σ_8=0.86 (+0.13/-0.10); S_8=0.77 (+0.10/-0.08), consistent with the AMICO KiDS-1000 number counts and with several external datasets.
Figure of merit improves by a factor 1.8 over the KiDS-DR3 AMICO clustering analyses, mainly from a tighter Ω_m; there is a ~2σ tension in Ω_m with Planck18 and with the DR3 w(θ) result.
Effective bias rises with redshift: 2.40, 2.89 and 3.68 in the three bins, with 15–17% uncertainties.

Photo-z errors dominate the small-scale damping and shift signal into the quadrupole and hexadecapole. AMICO's Δz=0.01 discretisation destabilises the higher multipoles at small scales, while FoG is negligible.
The authors suggest extending to KiDS-Legacy, Euclid and LSST, and eventually to alternative cosmologies.

papers.title: Cluster connectivity in DES Y3 data: impact on galaxy properties
papers.authors: C. Gouin, C. Laigle, J. Prat, L. O.V. Edwards, P. Ganeshaiah Veena, D. Galárraga-Espinosa, G. Gopidas
papers.abstract: Connectivity, namely the number of cosmic filaments reaching out of groups or clusters, has recently emerged as an informative way to quantify environment. With the advent of wide-area photometric surveys, it becomes possible to measure connectivity on a statistically significant sample of clusters. In this work, we extract the cosmic web from the DES Y3 photometric data and measure the connectivity around clusters from several public catalogs up to $z < 1$. Cosmic filaments are extracted in 2D with DisPerSE (the parametrization of which is calibrated on simulations) in tomographic slices of fixed comoving thickness of 220 Mpc, with a constant sampling across the redshift range ($\sim 0.1$ galaxies Mpc$^{-2}$). We first recover the well-established trend that cluster connectivity increases with cluster mass at all redshifts. We then investigate the properties of cluster member galaxies and find that, at fixed mass, clusters with a higher fraction of red (elliptical) galaxies are more strongly connected to the cosmic web. Furthermore, by examining the radial profiles of the red and elliptical galaxy fractions, we obtain hints that galaxy populations may undergo pre-processing within filamentary structures before being accreted into clusters. Overall, we demonstrate that despite photometric redshift uncertainties and projection effects, our method allows for the quantification of the cosmic web environment around clusters in broad-band photometric surveys. This work is consistent with results based on the Euclid Quick Release 1 (Q1). We plan to publicly release the cluster connectivity catalog as well as the cosmic filament catalog.

ai.summary: The paper measures cluster connectivity (number of cosmic filaments reaching a cluster) in DES Y3 photometric data and asks how it relates to cluster galaxy populations. Filaments are extracted in 2D with DisPerSE in 15 tomographic slices of ~222 cMpc thickness at constant galaxy density. The persistence threshold (1.5σ) is calibrated on simulations, and 50 photo-z realisations propagate redshift uncertainty. Connectivity is measured around X-ray and SZ selected clusters (eRASS1, RASS, ACT, SPT) at z<0.9. At fixed mass, more connected clusters have higher red and elliptical fractions, and galaxies near filaments show an excess of red galaxies, which hints at filament pre-processing. The method is a test bed for Euclid and LSST.

At fixed mass, connectivity correlates positively with red fraction, with partial Pearson ρ≈0.17–0.23 (p down to ~1e-12) at z<0.6.
Connectivity correlates with elliptical fraction at fixed mass, with ρ≈0.21–0.22 at z<0.4. The signal drops at higher z, but a stricter morphology cut gives ρ=0.14 at 0.4<z<0.6.

Galaxies within 0.1 Mpc of filaments around clusters have higher red and elliptical fractions than the isotropic average, with a stronger effect for red. This suggests filament pre-processing affects colour more than morphology.
A filament catalogue and a cluster connectivity catalogue are to be released.

papers.title: Semi-Analytic Predictions for Strong-Lensing Perturbers in Cold and Self-Interacting Dark Matter
papers.authors: Jonathan Tekverk, Duncan K. Adams, Simon Birrer, Rouven Essig, Daniel Gilman
papers.abstract: Strong gravitational lensing is sensitive to the abundance and internal structure of dark matter halos, providing a probe of gravothermal evolution in self-interacting dark matter (SIDM). We combine semi-analytic cold dark matter (CDM) subhalo histories with a model for gravothermal evolution in SIDM to generate CDM and SIDM subhalo populations across SIDM parameter space. We predict their projected enclosed masses and deflection-based projected density slopes and compare them with three perturbers inferred through gravitational imaging in PJ011646, SDSS J0946+1006, and JVAS B1938+666. For SIDM model parameters $\sigma_0/m_\chi=147.1$ cm$^2$/g and $w=120$ km/s, SIDM subhalos reproduce all three perturbers more often than CDM subhalos. For PJ011646, we find ~0.6 cored SIDM subhalos per host matching the perturber, compared with ~0.002 in CDM, while core-collapsed subhalos are too steep. For SDSS J0946+1006, we find ~3 core-collapsed and ~0.004 cored SIDM subhalos per host, compared with none in 900 CDM realizations, although baryons, neglected here, may matter for such massive subhalos. For "detection V" in JVAS B1938+666, we find ~220 core-collapsed and ~20 cored SIDM subhalos per host within the $2\sigma$ posterior region, compared with ~0.2 in CDM; the CDM candidates require exceptionally early accretion, at median redshift $z\sim13$. Simultaneously reproducing all three perturbers requires $w\gtrsim10^2$ km/s, so that the massive (~$5.6\times10^{10}M_\odot$) progenitors of SDSS J0946+1006 candidates can collapse, and is achieved for $\sigma_0/m_\chi\gtrsim10^2$ cm$^2$/g in the parameter sets studied. Our results show how semi-analytic models can quantify how often subhalos reproduce individual perturbers in different dark matter models, and our modular framework can be readily updated as models of tidal stripping and late-stage gravothermal evolution in SIDM improve. (abridged)

ai.summary: The paper asks whether strong-lensing perturbers found by gravitational imaging (PJ011646, SDSS J0946+1006, JVAS B1938+666) are more naturally explained by CDM or self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) subhalos. The authors generate CDM subhalo populations in 10^13 Msun hosts with the semi-analytic code SatGen. They map these to SIDM using the parametric gravothermal model of Yang et al. (2024), which gives cored or core-collapsed profiles. For each subhalo they compute the projected enclosed mass and the deflection-based projected slope, and they count how often these fall in each perturber's posterior region. The framework is fast and modular, so it can scan SIDM parameter space and be updated as tidal stripping and late-stage collapse modelling improve.

SDSS J0946+1006: ~3 collapsed and ~0.004 cored SIDM subhalos per host, with no CDM matches in 900 realizations. Baryons are neglected and may matter for these massive (~5.6e10 Msun) progenitors.

papers.title: The Impact of Inclination, Redshift, and Mass Ratio Selection on Cosmological Constraints from Bright Sirens Beyond Conventional Fisher Approximations
papers.authors: Gustavo B. F. Lima, Rafael F. Aranha, Rodrigo S. Gonçalves
papers.abstract: Future generations of gravitational-wave observatories are projected to detect up to thousands bright siren events within a decade of operation. However, the precision of these cosmological forecasts depends heavily on the astrophysical assumptions embedded within the simulation pipelines. In this work, we systematically investigate the impact of variations in the binary mass ratio ($q$), the maximum observable inclination angle ($\iota_{\max}$), and the maximum redshift ($z_{\max}$) on the constraints of the Hubble constant ($H_0$) and the matter density parameter ($\Omega_m$). We perform our analyses based on the GWDALI framework, the GW Doublet Approximation, and the phenomenological waveform approximant IMRPhenomD. By adopting sets of non-spinning binary neutron star populations we explore the impact of astrophysical parameters on the constraints of cosmological parameters. Our results reveal a clear dichotomy in the observational requirements: while the statistical uncertainty on $H_0$ falls below the falls below approximately $1.3\%$ level for $N \ge 400$ events and drops under $0.9\%$ once $N \ge 800$, a deep-redshift catalog ($z_{\max} \ge 1.0$) is strictly required to effectively break parameter degeneracies and constrain the global geometry through $\Omega_m$. Furthermore, expanding the maximum inclination cutoff from the conservative $20^{\circ}$ up to $40^{\circ}$ substantially mitigates the correlation between distance and inclination.

Using the GWDALI framework (a Fisher plus higher-order "doublet" likelihood approximation) with the IMRPhenomD waveform and non-spinning BNS populations, they vary the mass ratio q, the maximum inclination for a detectable counterpart (20° vs up to 40°), and the maximum redshift z_max. A large part of the text reviews the PhenomD waveform construction. The goal is to show how selection assumptions propagate into cosmological forecasts.

Raising the maximum inclination cutoff from 20° to 40° substantially reduces the distance-inclination correlation.

Systematics from waveform and selection modelling are expected to dominate over statistical errors in the 3G era.

papers.title: Introducing the GION Lightcone Simulation Suite for Multi-Wavelength Large-Scale Structure Cosmology
papers.authors: Ken Osato, Satoshi Tanaka, Tomoaki Ishiyama, Hironao Miyatake, Takahiro Nishimichi, Masato Shirasaki
papers.abstract: We present the GION (Ginkaku Lightcone Multi-wavelength Simulation Project) simulation suite: 10 full-sky high-resolution cosmological lightcone simulations and their associated products for multi-wavelength large-scale structure cosmology. We use the TreePM $N$-body code GINKAKU, which is highly optimized in the massively parallel environment, and integrate the on-the-fly lightcone construction technique. Each lightcone simulation is run with $6144^3$ particles in a volume of $(1.5 \, h^{-1} \, \mathrm{Gpc})^3$, which corresponds to a particle mass of $1.28 \times 10^9 \, h^{-1} \, \mathrm{M}_\odot$, and extends to $z = 5$. The fine mass resolution and the depth of the lightcone simulations allow us to resolve dark matter halos down to $10^{11} \, h^{-1} \, \mathrm{M}_\odot$ in the high-redshift Universe, which is crucial for applications to the Stage-IV cosmological surveys. The fundamental statistics of the simulations, including the matter power spectrum, halo power spectrum, and halo mass function, are validated against theoretical predictions. We also generate various large-scale structure observables from the lightcone outputs: the dark matter halo catalogs, mock galaxy samples, weak lensing convergence maps, and thermal and kinematic Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (tSZ and kSZ) maps. The angular power spectra of these observables, including the cross-correlation between weak lensing and the tSZ effect, are in good agreement with theoretical predictions, demonstrating that the suite provides mutually consistent multi-wavelength observables on the same lightcone. The GION simulation suite will be publicly available and can be used for various cosmological analyses to address the observational systematic effects and validate theoretical models.

From these the authors build halo catalogs, DESI-like mock LRG/ELG samples, Born-approximation convergence maps, and tSZ and kSZ maps. They validate the matter power spectrum, halo mass function, halo bias, and the angular spectra of all observables, including the kappa-y cross-correlation, against emulator, halo-model and perturbative predictions. The data will be released publicly. The suite is LCDM only (Planck 2018) and is intended as a testbed for Stage-IV and CMB joint analyses.

Cost is ~7.8e4 s per realization on 8192 Fugaku nodes; data volume is 10.1 TB per realization. Limitations: single cosmology, dark matter only, Born approximation, box replication.

papers.title: Luminosity-weighted galaxy and gravitational wave cross-correlations
papers.authors: Charles Dalang, Isabela Santiago de Matos, João Ferri, Raul Abramo, Tessa Baker
papers.abstract: Cross-correlations of galaxies and gravitational waves (GW) can be used to extract cosmological parameters and the gravitational wave bias. In this work, we study how to include galaxy luminosities in these spatial cross-correlations, inspired by the standard approach of dark sirens line-of-sight redshift priors. We present a formalism to include luminosity information in galaxy-GW simulations and study the effects of assigning a hosting probability that depends on luminosity through a simple power law $p_{\rm{host}} \propto L^\beta$ with $\beta \in \{0,1,2\}$ corresponding to uniformly, linear and quadratically weighted in luminosity. This effectively changes the GW linear bias with respect to dark matter and, in principle, allows to gain signal-to-noise and a sharper measurement of cosmological parameters. For a realistic luminosity dependence of the galaxy bias taken from DESI data, the gain is marginal, making the method robust to different luminosity weighting prescriptions. We show that the cross-correlation inference is able to recover the injected GW bias within $10\%$ if there is a mismatch between the injected linear bias of host galaxies and observed galaxies, provided that one sticks to relatively large scales. We also show that the Hubble constant and matter energy density can be recovered to $0.5\%$ and $5\%$ respectively with a third generation network of GW detectors, regardless of the modeling of the GW bias.

ai.summary: The paper asks how weighting galaxies by luminosity affects galaxy–gravitational-wave (GW) cross-correlation cosmology (the "Peak Sirens" method). The authors split DESI DR1 Bright Galaxies into 5 equi-populated luminosity bins, measure a bias for each, and build GLASS lightcone simulations with per-bin bias. Binary black hole hosts are sampled with $p_{\rm host}\propto L^\beta$, $\beta=0,1,2$. Mock ET+2CE GW catalogues (~70,000 sources) are cross-correlated with the weighted galaxy maps, using a rescaling technique to evaluate other cosmologies and a Gaussian likelihood. With realistic DESI biases the effective bias barely changes, so constraints on $H_0$, $\Omega_m$ and the GW bias are insensitive to $\beta$. The method also recovers the GW bias when the true hosts have a different bias than the observed galaxies, but only at large scales.

The SNR scales with the product of the galaxy bias squared and the GW bias, $b_g^2 b_{gw}$, so the uncertainties shrink as the injected $b_{gw}$ increases.
At $\ell_{\rm max}=110$ the injected GW bias is recovered to ~10% even with a host/observed bias mismatch, with $\sigma_{H_0}/H_0\approx2\%$ and $\sigma_{\Omega_m}/\Omega_m\approx26\%$.
At $\ell_{\rm max}=190$ the GW bias becomes biased (probably nonlinearity and scale dependence), but $H_0$ and $\Omega_m$ are still recovered within $1\sigma$, at 0.5% and 5% for ET+2CE.

papers.title: Joint Angular-Power Distributions of Interfering Nanohertz Gravitational Waves
papers.authors: Yan-Chen Bi, Yu-Mei Wu, Qing-Guo Huang
papers.abstract: Finite populations of supermassive black-hole binaries produce fluctuations in both gravitational-wave power and pulsar timing correlations. We characterize the realization-dependent, orientation-averaged Earth-term angular correlation through its frequency-resolved Legendre coefficients. A hybrid model of bright sources and a Gaussian faint background extends the conditional Gamma distribution in the many-weak-source limit to non-central $\chi^2$ statistics, yielding correlated multipoles after population marginalization. Our analytical variance decomposition and SMBHB population simulations reveal a population-dependent transition from interference dominated variance at low frequencies to population-power-dominated variance at high frequencies. In the many-weak-source regime, a multivariate lognormal approximation captures the main features of the joint distribution using only the first two log-cumulants. These results provide statistical benchmarks for fluctuations in both the overall amplitude and angular structure of the realized correlation.

ai.summary: The paper asks how a finite population of supermassive black-hole binaries makes the realized pulsar-timing angular correlation fluctuate around the Hellings–Downs curve. The authors decompose the orientation-averaged Earth-term correlation into Legendre coefficients $S_\ell$, each split into a total-power term and a wave-interference term. They model the many-weak-source limit with a conditional Gamma law, then add one bright source plus a Gaussian faint background, which gives a non-central $\chi^2$ law. They marginalize over the Poisson source population to obtain joint multipole distributions and covariances, and they derive a multivariate lognormal approximation. They test all of this against Monte Carlo SMBHB populations.

The covariance of $S_\ell$ splits into an interference term, which is diagonal in $\ell$, and a total-power variance term that correlates different multipoles.
Variance is interference-dominated at low frequencies and population-power-dominated at high frequencies. The crossover depends on the population model.
The non-central $\chi^2$ model matches the simulated variances at all frequencies, while the Gamma model fails at high frequencies.
A multivariate lognormal built from the first two log-cumulants captures the main features of the joint distribution at low frequencies, though it is less accurate than the full model.

papers.title: Modelling kNN-CDFs of biased tracers in redshift space using hybrid Lagrangian bias expansion
papers.authors: Eishica Chand, Arka Banerjee
papers.abstract: Higher-order statistics are becoming increasingly useful in clustering studies of the large-scale structure (LSS) of the universe. The kNN-CDFs are one such higher-order statistic, sensitive to all N-point correlations and easy to compute on data. Utilising their statistical gains for cosmological inference requires modelling them accurately for the tracer of interest. We use the hybrid Lagrangian bias expansion to enable this modelling in redshift space, building and validating the pipeline on Quijote simulations. We show that the kNN-CDFs of a luminous red galaxy (LRG)-like sample can be modelled down to scales as small as r = 10 Mpc/h, with the minimum reliable scale increasing with nearest-neighbour order. Moreover, the model parameters inferred from the kNN-CDFs also describe the galaxy power spectrum P(k), indicating model consistency across the two statistics and the feasibility of combining them. Fisher forecasts for galaxy auto clustering show that combining P(k) and kNN-CDFs improves constraints on all parameters relative to either statistic alone. Relative to P(k), the constraints on $b_3$ improve the most, while those on $\sigma_8$ and $\Omega_m$ improve by factors of 3.5 and 1.7, respectively. Including galaxy-matter cross clustering alongside galaxy auto clustering further improves the Fisher constraints from both P(k) and kNN-CDFs, with their combination yielding the tightest constraints overall. Relative to P(k), the largest improvement from this combination is found for $b_2$, while the constraints on $\sigma_8$ and $\Omega_m$ improve by factors of 4.2 and 1.7, respectively. These results demonstrate the applicability of the hybrid Lagrangian bias framework to model the kNN-CDFs of biased tracers in redshift space, and the potential of combining higher-order and two-point statistics to extract cosmological information.

Lagrangian bias operators (1, δ, δ², s², ∇²δ, plus δ³) are advected with Quijote N-body displacements, and RSDs are added through central distortion (halo velocities) plus an exponential Finger-of-God kernel with a satellite fraction. The model is validated on an HOD LRG-like sample at z=0.5 from Quijote. The authors then run Fisher forecasts for bias, FoG and cosmological parameters, combining kNN-CDFs with P(k) for galaxy auto and galaxy-matter cross clustering.

Parameters fitted to kNN-CDFs also describe real- and redshift-space P(k), but P(k)-fitted parameters do not reproduce the kNN-CDFs.

An emulator for kNN-CDFs and simulation-based inference are planned, and the unphysical δ_T<-1 regions are noted as a limitation of the hybrid framework.

papers.title: Non-Markovian Cosmology with Causal Memory Kernels
papers.authors: Aritra Sanyal, Prabir Rudra
papers.abstract: We investigate a non-Markovian extension of Friedmann cosmology in which the present expansion rate retains information about the past cosmic evolution through a causal memory kernel, with \LCDM{} recovered in the limit of vanishing kernel amplitude, $A\to0$. We show that five kernels (Linear, Power Law, Exponential, Gaussian and Oscillatory) arise as cosine transforms of the spectral densities of an unresolved hidden sector, and that the Exponential and Linear kernels also follow independently from Israel-Stewart causal viscosity and from Deser-Woodard non-local gravity, respectively. The Linear amplitude is consistent with zero ($A=0.002\pm0.030$ for CC+DR2). The Power-law, Exponential and Gaussian kernels are observationally degenerate: the data select sharply peaked kernels that constrain only an integrated amplitude $\Aeff\simeq0.01$--$0.03$, equivalent to a uniform $0.5$--$1.5\%$ rescaling of $H(z)$, and they are disfavoured relative to \LCDM{} ($\Delta{\rm AIC}=+2.5$ to $+3.6$). Only the Oscillatory kernel improves the fit appreciably ($\dchi=4.5$--$8.1$), but it requires a negative damping rate, which is incompatible with the causal derivations, and it is not favoured once CC data are included ($\Delta{\rm BIC}=+4.4$ to $+6.2$)

papers.title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks vs U-Net: Application to thermal dust emission recovery in the microwave
papers.authors: Nicolas Morant Juan, José M. Casas, Laura Bonavera
papers.abstract: Galactic thermal dust emission is the dominant foreground contaminant of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) at frequencies above 100 GHz, and its accurate separation is essential for current and future CMB experiments. Deep learning methods, in particular convolutional architectures such as the U-Net, have demonstrated strong performance for CMB component separation, but typically operate as purely data-driven models with no explicit enforcement of the physical laws governing the emission they reconstruct. In this work, we present a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) that embeds the Modified Black Body (MBB) spectral model as a hard, differentiable architectural constraint, and we compare it against a standard U-Net baseline trained under an identical pipeline. Both architectures are trained on realistic simulated Planck HFI patches at four frequencies (143, 217, 353 and 545 GHz) and evaluated on a shared validation set as well as on three independent Galactic dust realizations from the PySM phenomenological dust models named D4, D7 and D10. We find that both networks achieve comparable reconstruction quality across all evaluated datasets, with a Structural Similarity Index Measure consistently above 0.96 and a fitted angular power-spectrum spectral index that agrees with the input to within 1% in every region. Embedding the physical constraint in the PINN does not measurably degrade reconstruction accuracy relative to the unconstrained U-Net, while additionally guaranteeing that every predicted output corresponds to a thermodynamically admissible physical configuration. These results establish the physics-informed formulation as a viable methodological alternative for dust component separation, providing physical interpretability without a trade-off in reconstruction fidelity.

papers.title: Finite-distance effects and scalar suppression in massive gravity
papers.authors: Chris Choi, Tina Kahniashvili, Barnabás Póczos
papers.abstract: Pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) probe the stochastic gravitational wave (GW) background through the angular cross-correlations of timing residuals. For a GW background in general relativity (GR), the expected overlap reduction function (ORF) is given by the Hellings--Downs (HD) correlation. We investigate how a nonzero graviton mass modifies this prediction through a massive dispersion relation and additional vector and scalar polarizations, producing a modified effective ORF. In the massive limit, the finite-distance pulsar terms survive angular averaging, multiplying the correlations of all three polarization sectors by a pulsar-dependent factor that can enhance, suppress, or reverse them. We adopt a tensor Earth--Earth normalization that preserves the continuous finite-distance effect. In the massless limit, we find that the vector ORF vanishes and the scalar ORF approaches a finite breathing mode. We propose the phenomenological prescription $\Omega_S/\Omega_T=A_S(m_g/\omega)^{n_S}$, with scalar amplitude parameter $A_S$ and suppression index $n_S>0$. These results provide a consistent framework for future PTA analyses of massive gravity.

They derive the receiving functions analytically. They find that the vector ORF vanishes as $m_g\to0$, while the scalar ORF tends to a finite breathing-mode correlation. To recover GR in this limit they propose a phenomenological suppression $\Omega_S/\Omega_T=A_S(m_g/\omega)^{n_S}$. No PTA data analysis is done; this is a theory framework for future work.

The prescription $\Omega_S/\Omega_T=A_S(m_g/\omega)^{n_S}$ with $n_S>0$ decouples the scalar and recovers the GR tensor ORF as $m_g\to0$.

papers.title: Local Analogs of Little Red Dots: Clues to the X-ray Weakness
papers.authors: Shi-Jiang Chen, Jun-Xian Wang, Zhen-Ya Zheng, Ruqiu Lin, Luis C. Ho, Zhen-Yi Cai, Chang-Hao Chen, Zsofi Igo, Jia-Lai Kang, Ruancun Li, Teng Liu, Wenke Ren, Zhen-Bo Su
papers.abstract: A major question about JWST's little red dots (LRDs) at $z\sim4-8$ is the origin of their apparent X-ray weakness. Even deep Chandra stacks yield only tentative detections or broad-band limits and cannot distinguish among super-Eddington accretion, intrinsic X-ray weakness, and Compton-thick (CT) obscuration. Local analogs offer a powerful complementary route. At $z\sim0.3$, similarly luminous sources require $\sim10^{3-4}$ less exposure for comparable signal-to-noise, suffer less source confusion, and directly probe the diagnostic rest-frame soft X-rays. Here we present a pilot Einstein Probe/FXT study of six "local little red dots" (LLRDs), V-shaped broad-line green pea galaxies selected as low-redshift counterparts of LRDs. These sources show X-ray diversity: "X-normal" LLRDs resemble type 1 AGNs in X-ray luminosity and optical variability, whereas the "X-weak" stack lies $\sim0.5-0.7$ dex below standard unobscured-quasar scaling relations while remaining compatible with the representative LRD stack and 95% of published individual limits. The X-weak LLRDs also lack detected optical variability and have redder optical continua than X-normal LLRDs, making their V-shaped SEDs closer to those of high-redshift LRDs. The detection of the X-weak stack at $\sim3.3\sigma$ with the soft-X-ray-sensitive EP-FXT provides rest-frame $\sim2-3$ keV constraints difficult to reconcile with a typical unobscured super-Eddington model or a local-AGN-like CT geometry examined here, although modified variants remain possible. The simplest alternative is a mildly X-ray-weak corona ($\Delta\alpha_{\mathrm{ox}}\sim-0.1$ to $-0.2$) with Compton-thin absorption ($N_{\mathrm{H}}\sim10^{22-23}$ cm$^{-2}$), consistent with the independent Balmer decrement/break diagnostics. Together with growing samples of local LRD analogs, our results offer a practical path for testing the physical nature of LRD X-ray weakness.

papers.title: Stochastic dynamics of cosmological inflation in general relativity
papers.authors: Yoann L. Launay
papers.abstract: The theory of Inflation, supplemented by fluctuations of the quantum vacuum, is the leading paradigm to explain the correlations of inhomogeneities at very large distances in the Universe. Particle physics methods fail when strong non-linearity and non-perturbativity are involved, leaving a whole landscape of untestable scenarios of inflation. Starobinsky's stochastic inflation can in principle treat inflationary inhomogeneities nonlinearly and classically as the Hubble radius becomes smaller than their wavelengths, but it was never formulated in full general relativity, which motivates this thesis. Using the Keldysh formalism of nonequilibrium quantum field theory, we first develop a validity criterion for the use of classical computations, and thus simulations, to probe inflationary interactions, finding analytically that the bispectrum can be extracted from slightly sub-Hubble scales in quasi-de Sitter spacetimes. We then provide the first analytical solutions to the constraints for inhomogeneous initial conditions of numerical relativity simulations of inflation, and use them to explore its nonperturbative regime. Our main contribution is to obtain stochastic equations for the full set of inflaton equations in general relativity: this description incorporates the full nonlinear and backreacting evolution, is small-gauge-invariant, and is free of historical assumptions such as the gradient-free separate universe approximation. We implement these equations in the BSSN formulation of numerical relativity, demonstrating their correctness in slow-roll and ultra slow-roll scenarios via the satisfaction of the constraints, with a first look at eternal inflation. Finally, we extend our coarse-graining methods beyond General Relativity and single-field inflation, offering a phenomenological framework with the ambition of serving as a numerical particle collider for the early universe.

They are implemented in BSSN and validated through constraint satisfaction in slow-roll and ultra-slow-roll cases, with a first look at eternal inflation. papers.title: Gauge-field energy density in inflationary kinetic-coupling models: QFT regularization versus horizon cutoffs
papers.authors: A.O. Naidenko, O.O. Sobol, S.I. Vilchinskii
papers.abstract: Coupling gauge fields to the inflaton can amplify their quantum fluctuations during inflation, with potential applications to a range of cosmological phenomena. A central challenge is to define finite and physically meaningful observables, such as the gauge-field energy density. In this work, we study an Abelian gauge field kinetically coupled to the inflaton through $f^2(\phi)F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$ in a de Sitter background with $f\propto a^{\gamma_1}$, and compare conventional quantum-field-theoretic regularization with horizon-cutoff prescriptions. Using a hard physical-momentum cutoff and dimensional regularization, we derive the ultraviolet divergences in closed form and fix the remaining one-parameter finite-part ambiguity by requiring the coupling-induced total energy density to be nonnegative. We then examine five horizon-cutoff prescriptions based on characteristic scales of the mode equations. Their predictions depend sensitively on the choice of horizon scale and, for weak gauge-field production, can deviate substantially from the regularized result; for the adopted finite-part prescription, the minimal horizon agrees best with the regularized total energy density. As $|\gamma_1|\to 2$, where infrared modes dominate, the relative deviation of all prescriptions from the regularized result vanishes, independently of the finite-part prescription. Outside this regime, the separate electric and magnetic contributions, which can become negative after regularization, are not reliably reproduced by any of the horizon-cutoff prescriptions.

They then compare this result with five horizon-cutoff prescriptions that are common in the magnetogenesis and backreaction literature. The separate electric and magnetic energy densities can become negative after regularization, and no horizon prescription reproduces them reliably.

papers.title: The Galactic Center Gamma-Ray Excess and the Look-Elsewhere Effect
papers.authors: Isabel S. Sands, Philip F. Hopkins
papers.abstract: The origin of the excess of GeV gamma-rays in the Milky Way's galactic center observed by Fermi-LAT has been an open question for nearly two decades. The two leading interpretations of this signal are that it is produced either by annihilating dark matter (DM), or arises from unresolved point sources, such as a novel population of millisecond pulsars. In both scenarios, uncertainties and limitations in the modeling of galactic diffuse gamma-ray emission, such as the steady-state approximation of cosmic ray (CR) propagation and assumption of an axisymmetric distribution of CRs, complicate the interpretation of the galactic center excess (GCE). Simulations with full magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) and CR transport can provide a new avenue for understanding the astrophysical phenomena that drive galactic diffuse gamma-ray emission. We utilize MHD simulations of Milky Way analogs with time-dependent, spectrally-resolved CR transport to reconstruct diffuse gamma-ray emission. Comparing instantaneous emission to a time-averaged baseline, we find residuals up to several times larger than the Fermi GCE, with a wide range of spectral shapes and spatial morphologies. At some simulation snapshots, the spectrum and morphology of the residuals resemble the Fermi GCE. Our results suggest that the Fermi GCE may be a manifestation of the look-elsewhere effect- a transient fluctuation in diffuse emission from stellar sources, observed at an inopportune moment- and motivate the development of new Fermi-LAT analysis templates that account for time-dependent CR transport.

The residuals vary widely in spectrum and morphology, and some snapshots resemble the GCE. This suggests that static templates (e.g. GALPROP) may underestimate astrophysical uncertainties. The sample is small, and the simulated central star formation rates are too high.

papers.title: Natural Inflation with Exponentially Small Tensor-To-Scalar Ratio
papers.authors: Dario L. Lorenzoni, David I. Kaiser, Evan McDonough
papers.abstract: We demonstrate that "natural inflation", also known as "axion inflation", can be compatible with Planck 2018 measurements of the cosmic microwave background, while predicting an exponentially small tensor-to-scalar ratio, e.g., $r\sim 10^{-15}$. The strong suppression of $r$ arises from dynamics of the radial component of the complex scalar field, whose phase is the axion. Such tiny values of $r$ remain well below the threshold for detection by CMB-S4 or Simons Observatory B-mode searches. The model is testable with the running $\alpha_s$ of the spectral index, which is within reach of next-generation CMB and large-scale structure experiments, motivating the running as a primary science goal for future experiments.

papers.title: Resilience of Primordial Black Hole Formation from Inflation with a Light Spectator Field
papers.authors: Dario L. Lorenzoni, Sarah R. Geller, Zachary Ireland, David I. Kaiser, Evan McDonough, Kyle A. Wittmeier
papers.abstract: Scalar fields are ubiquitous in theories of high-energy physics. In the context of cosmic inflation, this suggests the existence of spectator fields, which provide a subdominant source of energy density. We show that spectator fields boost the inflationary production of primordial black holes, with single-field ultra-slow-roll evolution supplanted by a phase of evolution along the spectator direction, and primordial perturbations amplified by the resulting multifield dynamics. This generic mechanism is largely free from the severe fine-tuning that afflicts single-field inflationary PBH models.

papers.title: Primordial Black Holes from Inflation with a Spectator Field
papers.authors: Dario L. Lorenzoni, Sarah R. Geller, David I. Kaiser, Evan McDonough
papers.abstract: How is the production of primordial black holes (PBHs) in single-field models of inflation impacted by the presence of additional scalar fields? We consider the effect of a spectator field - a free scalar field with sub-Hubble mass and no direct coupling to the inflaton and which makes a subdominant contribution to the total energy density - in the context of single-field models of inflation featuring a transient phase of ultra-slow-roll evolution. Despite the modest title, a spectator field can have a dramatic impact: the slow-roll evolution of the spectator prevents the combined inflaton-and-spectator system from entering into ultra-slow-roll, which naively might be expected to preclude the production of PBHs. However, we demonstrate that the growth of perturbations is maintained or enhanced by the spectator, through the rich interplay of curvature and isocurvature perturbations. We show in a model-independent way that the single-field phase of ultra-slow-roll is replaced by two turns in field space encompassing a phase of tachyonic instability for the isocurvature perturbations and a transfer of power from isocurvature to curvature modes. Furthermore, we highlight a degeneracy between the fine-tuning of the feature in the inflaton potential and the parameters of the spectator, leading to an overall resilience of model predictions to parameter variations. This makes it easier for the underlying PBH model to accommodate both high-precision cosmic microwave background constraints and production of PBHs in the asteroid-mass range.

papers.title: Cosmological Equivalence of Scalar-Tensor-Vector Modified Gravity and Cold Dark Matter
papers.authors: John W. Moffat
papers.abstract: We show that Scalar-Tensor-Vector Gravity (STVG-MOG) is observationally equivalent to the standard model $\Lambda$CDM cosmological model for all probes that depend on isotropic and linear gravitational dynamics, including galaxy rotation curves, cluster lensing, the linear matter power spectrum P(k), $\sigma_8$, baryon acoustic oscillations, and the cosmic microwave background (CMB). This degeneracy arises from the scale-dependent effective gravitational coupling $G_{\mathrm{eff}}$, which ensures identical background evolution, transfer functions, and linear growth. Consequently, all early-universe, low and intermediate scale cosmological observables are equally well described by STVG-MOG without invoking non-baryonic dark matter. We argue that the equivalence implies that isotropic cosmological data alone cannot establish the physical existence of dark matter. The degeneracy is broken only by observables sensitive to large-scale, anisotropic gravitational response. In particular, recent measurements of enhanced radio-galaxy and quasar number-count dipoles at gigaparsec scales probe a regime where $G_{\mathrm{eff}}$ departs from its $\Lambda$CDM limit, allowing STVG-MOG to generate anisotropic bulk flows, while preserving consistency with all isotropic constraints. These observations provide a concrete pathway for empirically distinguishing modified gravity from particle dark matter.

papers.title: Kinematic cosmic dipole from a large sample of strong lenses
papers.authors: Martin Millon, Charles Dalang, Thomas Collett, Camille Bonvin
papers.abstract: Measurements of the kinematic cosmic dipole continue to show an intriguing tension between the value inferred from the CMB and that obtained from high-redshift source number counts. While the measured dipole direction appears consistent, the amplitude, set by the observer's peculiar velocity $v_{o}$, remains in significant disagreement. In this paper, we propose using strong gravitational lenses with well-measured Einstein radii to estimate the kinematic cosmic dipole, through the relativistic aberration of the Einstein angle induced by the observer's motion. We show that this effect could be detected solely from measurements of the Einstein radius in wide, high-resolution imaging surveys such as Euclid. However, the precision achievable using Einstein-radius measurements alone, without redshift or lens-galaxy mass information, appears insufficient to discriminate between the CMB value of $v_{o}$ and that derived from source number counts at high statistical significance. Nevertheless, we demonstrate that including a large sample of lenses with available kinematic information, either via the Fundamental Plane relation or, ideally, through spectroscopic velocity-dispersion measurements, drastically reduces the noise and substantially improves the constraining power of this method. We show that, for a realistic sample of strong lenses detected by Euclid and complemented with spectroscopic velocity dispersion measurements from 4MOST or DESI, it is possible to discriminate between the CMB- and source-number-counts-inferred values at the $\sim 5\sigma$ level using a new, fully independent method. We further demonstrate that this technique is only weakly sensitive to strong-lensing selection effects, with selection biases and threshold effects estimated to be well below the 1% level.

papers.title: Effective reheating in Gauss--Bonnet inflation with $μ(ϕ,X)$ coupling
papers.authors: Ali Seidabadi, Sara Saghafi, Kourosh Nozari
papers.abstract: We study effective reheating in a scalar--Gauss--Bonnet inflationary model with a phase-space-dependent coupling $\mu(\phi,X)$, in which a compact field-space feature is combined with a bounded kinetic gate. The modified inflationary background determines the pivot-scale quantities and the effective energy density at the end of inflation. These quantities are then used to derive the reheating duration $N_{\rm re}$ and temperature $T_{\rm re}$ through the thermal-history matching relation. We first perform two fixed-pivot reference scans by varying the overall Gauss--Bonnet strength $\lambda_{\rm GB}$ and the kinetic parameter $g_{_X}$ separately. For the reference parameter choices, increasing either parameter increases $N_{\rm re}$ and decreases $T_{\rm re}$ for the selected reheating equations of state. Additional benchmark calculations clarify how these variations depend on the dynamical regime of the model. In the $\lambda_{\rm GB}$ scan, the increase in $N_{\rm re}$ and the decrease in $T_{\rm re}$ persist, although both variations become strongly suppressed when the coupling is more localized or when the end of inflation is controlled more strongly by the E-model potential. In the $g_{_X}$ scan, stronger field-space localization and kinetic saturation can instead lead to a slight decrease in $N_{\rm re}$ and an increase in $T_{\rm re}$ as $g_{_X}$ is increased. When the bounded kinetic contribution is considered together with a weaker overall Gauss--Bonnet interaction, the resulting changes in the reheating quantities become nearly negligible. The fixed-pivot predictions of the representative and alternative benchmarks are compared with CMB this http URL reheating constraints are then discussed for four representative values of the effective equation-of-state parameter, $\overline{w}_{\rm re}=-1/3,0,2/3,$ and $1$.

papers.title: AXIS Could Have Accessed Dark Matter Decays
papers.authors: Joshua W. Foster, Inci Karaaslan, Gordan Krnjaic, Nimrod Shapir
papers.abstract: The Advanced X-ray Imaging Satellite (AXIS) was a mission concept designed to improve upon the sensitivity and spatial resolution of the Chandra X-ray Observatory and XMM-Newton. Although AXIS was not selected for implementation, the concept study defined a mature instrument design with low-background, arcsecond imaging over the $0.3$-$10$ keV energy range, a large effective area, and a wide field of view. These capabilities provide a useful benchmark for the dark matter decay sensitivity of future X-ray observatories. We estimate the reach of a future AXIS-like instrument for narrow photon lines from decaying keV-scale dark matter, including axion-like particles and sterile neutrinos. For Galactic center observations, we find projected lifetime sensitivities of order $10^{31}$ s, improving upon existing limits by up to an order of magnitude over part of the keV mass range.

papers.title: Tracing the Cosmic Origins: Machine Learning Reconstruction of the Primordial Density Field from EoR Observations
papers.authors: Anchal Saxena, P. Daniel Meerburg, Guochao Sun, Tzu-Ching Chang, Lluís Mas-Ribas
papers.abstract: Reconstructing the initial conditions of the Universe from late-time tracers would unlock cosmological information buried by non-linear structure formation and astrophysics. We reconstruct the initial density field corresponding to $z=300$, with its linear amplitude extrapolated to $z=0$, from simulated 21-cm and CO(1-0) line-intensity maps at $z=8$ generated with LIMFAST. Using a three-dimensional U-Net, we reconstruct the initial conditions and evaluate their impact on cosmological parameter constraints. The two tracers probe complementary environments: 21-cm emission traces neutral, low-density regions of the IGM, while CO traces overdense, star-forming regions. We also train and evaluate the reconstruction on maps incorporating SKA1-Low- and COMAP-ERA-like instrumental response and thermal noise. In the noiseless case, combining both tracers delivers the most accurate reconstruction across ionisation states, with the cross-correlation coefficient between the reconstructed and true initial density fields, $|C(k)| \gtrsim 0.90$ for $k \lesssim 0.75\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$. With observational effects, small-scale information is degraded, but the joint reconstruction retains substantial large-scale coherence, with $|C(k)| \gtrsim 0.70$ for $k \lesssim 0.3\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$. We quantify cosmological information gains through simulation-based inference using power-spectrum summaries pre- and post-reconstruction. The largest improvements occur for $\sigma_8$ and $n_{\rm s}$, with a median aggregate marginal compression of $1.17$ bits in the noiseless case, corresponding to a $56\%$ reduction in the factorised product of prior-normalised $68\%$ marginal widths. With observational effects, the corresponding median compression is $1.29$ bits. These results demonstrate that joint 21-cm-CO reconstruction recovers cosmological information beyond pre-reconstruction summaries.

papers.title: The Loud Tail of the Supermassive Black Hole Binary Population: Multimessenger Candidates and Prospects for SKAO
papers.authors: Juhan Raidal, Ville Vaskonen, Juan Urrutia, Hardi Veermäe
papers.abstract: We assess whether electromagnetically identified supermassive black hole (SMBH) binary candidates populate the rare, high-amplitude tail of the gravitational wave (GW) amplitude distribution. Using an SMBH binary population model fitted to the NANOGrav 15-year data, we find that 3C~66B and Mrk~501 are likely to stand out from the GW background, making them promising targets for individual-source searches. Furthermore, we show that individual detections can probe the binary hardening mechanism, as models with strong environmental hardening predict a higher abundance of individually resolvable binaries than purely GW-driven models. Applying the same population fits and accounting for the confusion noise from the unresolved population, we forecast that the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO) will resolve tens of individual binaries, with 3C~66B robustly detectable.

papers.title: CosmoAgent: AI Agent for Theoretical Cosmology
papers.authors: Stephon Alexander, Loukas Gouskos, Savvas M. Koushiappas, Cooper Niu, Wenrong Sun
papers.abstract: We present CosmoAgent, an agentic AI framework using large language models (LLMs) to search for dark-energy and modified-gravity models. We define a covariant grammar that allows LLM agents to explore the space of modified-gravity Lagrangians. An in-house computational pipeline derives the equations of motion, solves the background dynamics, and evaluates the likelihood using late-time expansion data, including the DES 5-year type Ia supernova sample and the DESI Data Release 2 BAO measurements. Theories are ranked by the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) to balance simplicity and likelihood. We benchmarked 8 frontier LLMs from ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Kimi, DeepSeek, and Qwen, and all LLMs are able to find theories with a lower nominal AIC than flat $\Lambda$CDM, with a best improvement of $\Delta$ AIC=-3.328. Seven recover quadratic quintessence. Exploratory searches also return induced-gravity and scalar-Gauss-Bonnet structures. The modest AIC improvements do not establish an observational preference for these models over flat $\Lambda$CDM. The code is publicly available at this https URL

papers.title: Dark Matter, Baryon Number, and Cosmic-Ray Antinuclei
papers.authors: Caleb Gemmell, Dan Hooper, Seth Koren, Fabrizio Vassallo
papers.abstract: Antideuterons and antihelium nuclei in the cosmic-ray spectrum have long been considered a smoking gun signature of dark matter annihilation, making the tentative observation of several such events by AMS highly intriguing. Conventional dark matter models, however, can produce only up to O(1) antideuteron events at AMS and are not capable of generating observable fluxes of antihelium. In this Letter, we propose a class of models in which dark matter annihilates into particles carrying baryon and lepton number, whose subsequent decays produce enhanced fluxes of antinucleons and antinuclei. Such scenarios are motivated by Grand Unified Theories and can lead to an order-of-magnitude or larger enhancement in the resulting antideuteron and antihelium-3 fluxes, providing a means by which to potentially explain the events reported by the AMS Collaboration.

papers.title: Toward Bayesian photometric cosmic chronometers: Application to VIPERS
papers.authors: Swaraj Pradhan, Pablo Renard, Enrique Gaztanaga, Malgorzata Siudek, Thibaud Moutard
papers.abstract: The cosmic chronometer (CC) method provides a direct measurement of the expansion history of the universe, $H(z)$, from the differential ages of passively evolving galaxies. However, most CC analyses rely on high-quality spectroscopy to select passive galaxies, measure age-sensitive spectral features, and control stellar-population systematics. We build on existing works that use the D4000 spectral break as a proxy for measuring galaxy ages and apply it to a photometry-selected galaxy sample from VIPERS PDR2 in the range $0.5 \le z \le 0.8$. Our goal is to extend the scope of the standard CC framework to photometric surveys. To achieve this, we first selected a massive and passive galaxy sample using rest-frame colors and mass. Second, we designed a Bayesian framework to infer full galaxy age posteriors in fine redshift bins, using a D4000-age-metallicity grid from stellar population synthesis models. We marginalized over metallicity, using a Gaussian metallicity prior to break the D4000-age-metallicity degeneracy. Subsequently, we derived age-difference posteriors between redshift bins by convolving their age posteriors. Finally, using the median and errors extracted from the differential age posteriors, we calculated the weighted average $H(z)$ over our selected redshift range. We obtain $H(z=0.65)=93.68\pm28.27\,{\rm (stat.)}\pm10.67\,{\rm (syst.)}\ {\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$, which is consistent with existing spectroscopic CC measurements and with the $\Lambda$ cold dark matter ($\Lambda$CDM) model prediction from Planck at the same redshift. This result provides a proof of concept for extending direct $H(z)$ measurements from cosmic chronometers to photometric and spectro-photometric surveys, where larger samples can compensate for lower spectral resolution, provided that passive-galaxy selection, metallicity priors, and stellar-population systematics are carefully controlled.

papers.title: Extra-dimensional Origins of Chemical Potentials at the Cosmological Collider
papers.authors: Raman Sundrum, Zhaohui Xu
papers.abstract: We study the realization of the chemical potential mechanism in cosmological collider physics in a robust class of inflationary models arising from multiple higher-dimensional gauge fields. The rolling inflaton background corresponds to an electric field in the extra dimension in which charged particles are produced analogously to the Schwinger mechanism, while neutral particles can be produced through non-minimal interactions. We show that particles heavier than the inflationary Hubble scale can be created without Boltzmann suppression in both cases. In particular, charged Kaluza-Klein excitations can be created through minimal gauge interactions. We construct realistic models along these lines consistent with both theoretical and experimental constraints.

papers.title: Direct detection of right-handed fermionic dark matter: electron-recoil measurements in Xe atoms
papers.authors: Santiago Collazo, Carlos Argüelles, Soroush Shakeri, Osvaldo Civitarese
papers.abstract: We present theoretical estimations of the event rates for the interaction between a right-handed fermionic dark matter with an electron bound to a xenon atom. Motivated by recent astrophysical and cosmological constraints on a fermionic dark matter candidate in the sub-MeV mass range, we study such an interaction through an effective electromagnetic channel where the output consists of standard-model particles. This mechanism allows right-handed neutral dark matter fermions to couple with standard-model particles with the interchange of $W^{\pm}$ or $Z$ bosons, without the need to add extra fields. We generalize and extend previous results on this type of channels, by including for the ionization form factor arising from the interaction of the fermionic candidate with bound electrons. In addition, we compute the sensitivity curves for different direct detection experiments in such a challenging light particle mass range.
